readings.title: Lines Composed a Few Miles above Tintern Abbey
readings.challenge: Follow one long verse paragraph through past, present and future, and track how the speaker’s relation to nature has changed.
readings.focus: Memory as a source of strength, and what growing older takes and gives.
readings.context: William Wordsworth (1770–1850) wrote the poems in this volume between 1798 and 1803; from 1799 he lived with his sister Dorothy at Grasmere in the English Lake District. He wrote this in July 1798, on a walking tour with Dorothy, on returning to the valley of the River Wye, on the border of Wales, five years after a first visit. Tintern Abbey is a ruined medieval monastery nearby; the poem never describes it. Copses are small woods; “sylvan” means wooded; a roe is a small deer; a cataract is a waterfall; “interfused” means blended through; “genial spirits” are natural cheerfulness. The poem ended Lyrical Ballads (1798), which he published with Coleridge.

excerpt.locator: Lines, composed a few miles above Tintern Abbey, the whole poem; opens “Five years have past; five summers, with the length Of five long winters! and again I…”; closes “…green pastoral landscape, were to me More dear, both for themselves and for thy sake!”.

questions.prompt: What has the memory of this landscape done for the speaker during his five years away?
facilitatorNotes: In tiring city rooms it brought calm “sensations sweet,” perhaps encouraged small unremembered kindnesses, and gave a “blessed mood” in which he could “see into the life of things.” Notice how carefully he hedges (“such, perhaps,” “I trust”): he claims only what he believes, not what he can prove.
evidence: In hours of weariness, sensations sweet,
His little, nameless, unremembered, acts Of kindness and of love.

questions.prompt: How was nature different for him as a young man? Why does he say he was “more like a man / Flying from something that he dreads”?
facilitatorNotes: Then nature was “an appetite,” a physical passion needing no thought. The flight image suggests restless, driven energy; the poem does not say what he fled, and readers can only speculate. The point is that his youthful love was urgent rather than reflective.
evidence: Flying from something that he dreads, than one Who sought the thing he loved.
An appetite; a feeling and a love,

questions.prompt: What has he gained in place of those “aching joys”? Is the exchange convincing?
facilitatorNotes: He now hears “the still, sad music of humanity” in nature and feels a “presence,” a spirit rolling through all things. Some readers find this a real gain; others notice “I would believe,” which suggests he is persuading himself as well as us.
evidence: The still, sad music of humanity,
A presence that disturbs me with the joy Of elevated thoughts;

questions.prompt: Why does the poem turn to his sister at the end? What does he hope her memories will do for her?
facilitatorNotes: In her “wild eyes” he sees what he was five years ago. He hopes the landscape will become a store of memories that heals her in solitude, fear or grief, as his memories healed him, even if he is no longer there. The poem becomes a gift to her.
evidence: May I behold in thee what I was once,
Thy memory be as a dwelling-place For all sweet sounds and harmonies;

readings.title: Influence of Natural Objects: skating at nightfall
readings.workTitle: Influence of Natural Objects in calling forth and strengthening the Imagination in Boyhood and Early Youth
readings.challenge: Follow a long sentence of rushing action, then the stillness that ends it.
readings.focus: How an ordinary winter game becomes, in memory, a meeting with something vast.
readings.context: William Wordsworth (1770–1850) wrote the poems in this volume between 1798 and 1803; from 1799 he lived with his sister Dorothy at Grasmere in the English Lake District. This passage, written in 1799 about his boyhood at school in Hawkshead in the Lake District, later became part of his long autobiographical poem, The Prelude. “Vouchsafed” means granted; “stinted” means stingy; “shod with steel” means wearing skates; “confederate” means joined together; the “reflex of a star” is its reflection on the ice; “diurnal” means daily.

excerpt.locator: Influence of Natural Objects in calling forth and strengthening the Imagination in Boyhood and Early Youth, the whole poem; opens “Wisdom and Spirit of the universe! Thou Soul, that art the Eternity of thought! And…”; closes “…Feebler and feebler, and I stood and watched Till all was tranquil as a summer sea.”.

questions.prompt: The poem opens by addressing the “Wisdom and Spirit of the universe.” What does the speaker say this spirit did for him as a child?
facilitatorNotes: It shaped his feelings through “high objects” of nature rather than mean human works, and even made pain and fear part of his growth, until he could feel “a grandeur” in his own heartbeat. The skating memory is offered as an example.
evidence: Not with the mean and vulgar works of Man: But with high objects, with enduring things,
A grandeur in the beatings of the heart.

questions.prompt: How do the sounds change through the long sentence that begins “So through the darkness and the cold we flew”?
facilitatorNotes: The boys’ din makes the cliffs ring and the icy trees tinkle “like iron”; then the distant hills send back “an alien sound / Of melancholy.” Nature answers the noise with something strange and sad that the boy notices even in his excitement.
evidence: Tinkled like iron;
Into the tumult sent an alien sound Of melancholy,

questions.prompt: Why does the boy leave the crowd to “cut across the reflex of a star”? What does he seem to want?
facilitatorNotes: He seeks a quiet bay and chases a star’s reflection that always flies ahead of him. He wants solitude, and perhaps something that cannot be caught; the image is playful and a little lonely.
evidence: Not seldom from the uproar I retired Into a silent bay,
To cut across the reflex of a star;

questions.prompt: When he stops short, the cliffs keep wheeling past. What is really happening, and why describe it as the earth turning?
facilitatorNotes: It is the dizziness of someone who has been spinning. Wordsworth turns the bodily illusion into a glimpse of the earth’s daily rotation made visible, then lets everything settle “tranquil as a summer sea.” A common sensation becomes a vision.
evidence: Wheeled by me—even as if the earth had rolled With visible motion her diurnal round!
Till all was tranquil as a summer sea.

readings.title: The Two April Mornings
readings.challenge: Keep track of three times in a short ballad: the walk, the morning thirty years before, and the speaker’s present.
readings.focus: How one remembered morning holds grief, love and a refusal.
readings.context: William Wordsworth (1770–1850) wrote the poems in this volume between 1798 and 1803; from 1799 he lived with his sister Dorothy at Grasmere in the English Lake District. Matthew, an old village schoolmaster, is the subject of several poems Wordsworth wrote in 1799. Rills are small streams; to “sue the sport” is to go after it, here fishing; a yew is an evergreen tree often grown in churchyards; wilding is a wild apple tree.

excerpt.locator: The Two April Mornings, the whole poem; opens “We walked along, while bright and red Uprose the morning sun; And Matthew stopped, he…”; closes “…now, Methinks, I see him stand, As at that moment, with a bough Of wilding in his hand.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Matthew sigh on such a beautiful morning?
facilitatorNotes: The cloud and the coloured sky are exactly like an April morning thirty years before, when he stopped by his daughter Emma’s grave. His opening “The will of God be done!” already shows a grief he has learned to accept.
evidence: Brings fresh into my mind A day like this which I have left Full thirty years behind.
Beside my daughter's grave.

questions.prompt: Why might Matthew have loved his dead daughter more on that day than ever before?
facilitatorNotes: The beauty of the morning, so like her own brightness, sharpened his loss and his love together. “For so it seemed” shows that he is reporting a feeling, not measuring it.
evidence: And yet I loved her more, For so it seemed, than till that day I e'er had loved before.

questions.prompt: Matthew meets a lovely, happy girl by the churchyard. Why does he “not wish her mine”?
facilitatorNotes: Several readings fit: no child could replace Emma; he could not bear to risk such a loss again; or he can delight in the girl’s happiness without wanting to possess it. The poem does not choose, and the exclamation mark leaves his feeling strong but unexplained.
evidence: I looked at her, and looked again: And did not wish her mine!

questions.prompt: The last stanza jumps forward: Matthew is now dead. How does the ending repeat the pattern of Matthew’s own story?
facilitatorNotes: As Matthew saw Emma again on a morning thirty years later, the speaker now sees Matthew, as he stood that day with a bough in his hand. Memory passes the grief and the love on, from one person to the next.
evidence: Matthew is in his grave, yet now, Methinks, I see him stand,

readings.title: The Fountain
readings.challenge: Follow a conversation between a young man and an old one, and notice what each misunderstands.
readings.focus: Age, loss and the duty to seem cheerful.
readings.context: William Wordsworth (1770–1850) wrote the poems in this volume between 1798 and 1803; from 1799 he lived with his sister Dorothy at Grasmere in the English Lake District. This is another poem about Matthew, the old village schoolmaster. A fountain here is a natural spring; a border-song is a ballad from the borders of Scotland and England; a catch is a song sung as a round; “of yore” means long ago; “approved” means respected.

excerpt.locator: The Fountain, the whole poem; opens “We talked with open heart, and tongue Affectionate and true, A pair of friends, though I…”; closes “…He sang those witty rhymes About the crazy old church-clock, And the bewildered chimes.”.

questions.prompt: The young man asks Matthew for a song. Why does Matthew answer with sadness instead?
facilitatorNotes: The spring will murmur on for a thousand years unchanged, while Matthew has aged; the same sound reminds him of the vigorous man he was when he lay there before.
evidence: 'Twill murmur on a thousand years, And flow as now it flows.
For the same sound is in my ears Which in those days I heard.

questions.prompt: “The wiser mind / Mourns less for what age takes away / Than what it leaves behind.” What does age leave behind that is worse than what it takes?
facilitatorNotes: Habit and memory: the duty of wearing “a face of joy” because one was once glad, and loneliness after the deaths of one’s family. Ask readers to restate the paradox in their own words before judging it.
evidence: We wear a face of joy, because We have been glad of yore.

questions.prompt: How are the birds different from people, according to Matthew?
facilitatorNotes: Birds sing when they please and are quiet when they will; they never quarrel with nature, so their old age is “beautiful and free.” People are “pressed by heavy laws,” including the expectation that they will go on being cheerful.
evidence: Let loose their carols when they please, Are quiet when they will.
But we are pressed by heavy laws;

questions.prompt: Matthew answers the offer of a son with “Alas! that cannot be,” yet the poem ends with him singing his witty rhymes. How do you read the ending?
facilitatorNotes: No friend can replace his dead children, but the friendship still lifts him. Some readers see real recovery; others see the very “face of joy” he described, worn out of habit and kindness. Both readings use his own words.
evidence: Alas! that cannot be.
He sang those witty rhymes

readings.title: Resolution and Independence
readings.challenge: Follow a mood that rises, falls and is steadied, and watch the poet’s attention drift during a conversation.
readings.focus: What a chance meeting teaches a frightened young poet, and how well he listens.
readings.context: William Wordsworth (1770–1850) wrote the poems in this volume between 1798 and 1803; from 1799 he lived with his sister Dorothy at Grasmere in the English Lake District. He wrote this in 1802 after meeting an old man who gathered leeches, small blood-sucking worms that doctors then used to draw blood; by then they were growing scarce. Thomas Chatterton (1752–1770) was a brilliant young poet who killed himself at seventeen; the poet “Following his plough” is Robert Burns, the Scottish farmer-poet, who died at thirty-seven. A stock-dove is a wild pigeon; “plashy” means splashy; “untoward” means troublesome; to con is to study; “grave Livers” are serious-living people; “admonishment” is warning or advice.
readings.contentNote: Stanza VII mentions a young poet’s suicide and poets who end in “despondency and madness.”

excerpt.locator: Resolution and Independence, the whole poem (stanzas I–XX); opens “There was a roaring in the wind all night; The rain came heavily and fell in floods; But…”; closes “…I, "be my help and stay secure; I'll think of the Leech-gatherer on the lonely moor!"”.

questions.prompt: The first three stanzas are full of joy. What happens in stanza IV, and what reason does the speaker give?
facilitatorNotes: His mood falls as far as it had risen, into “fears and fancies” he cannot name. He offers a rule of feeling rather than a cause: the higher our delight, the lower our dejection.
evidence: As high as we have mounted in delight In our dejection do we sink as low;
Dim sadness—and blind thoughts, I knew not, nor could name.

questions.prompt: What does he fear for his own future, and why do Chatterton and Burns come to mind?
facilitatorNotes: He has lived as if needful things would come unsought, and now wonders why anyone should provide for a man who takes no care of himself. The two poets show genius ending in poverty or despair: “We Poets in our youth begin in gladness.”
evidence: But how can He expect that others should Build for him, sow for him,
We Poets in our youth begin in gladness; But thereof come in the end despondency and madness.

questions.prompt: How does the poet describe the old man in stanzas IX–XI? Why compare him to a stone and a sea-beast?
facilitatorNotes: He seems part of the landscape, a boulder whose arrival no one can explain, or a creature halfway between rock and life, “not all alive nor dead.” The comparisons make the meeting feel strange and almost visionary.
evidence: As a huge stone is sometimes seen to lie
Such seemed this Man, not all alive nor dead,

questions.prompt: The speaker asks the same question twice and hardly hears the answer. What is odd about that, and what does he finally take from the meeting?
facilitatorNotes: Lost in his fears, he hears the old man’s voice as a stream, “nor word from word could I divide,” and must ask again. Yet he ends ashamed of himself, admiring “so firm a mind” in poverty and age. Some readers think he uses the poor man as a lesson for himself; others think his self-scorn shows real humility.
evidence: My question eagerly did I renew,
In that decrepit Man so firm a mind.

readings.title: Composed upon Westminster Bridge, September 3, 1802
readings.challenge: Read a sonnet slowly enough to notice what is unexpected about its subject and its hour.
readings.focus: A crowded city seen, for a moment, as a sleeping landscape.
readings.context: William Wordsworth (1770–1850) wrote the poems in this volume between 1798 and 1803; from 1799 he lived with his sister Dorothy at Grasmere in the English Lake District. He saw London from Westminster Bridge over the River Thames early one morning in 1802, while leaving the city with Dorothy. A sonnet is a poem of fourteen lines; here the first eight describe and the last six exclaim. To steep is to soak.

excerpt.locator: Composed upon Westminster Bridge, September 3, 1802, the whole sonnet; opens “Earth has not any thing to show more fair: Dull would he be of soul who could pass by A…”; closes “…will: Dear God! the very houses seem asleep; And all that mighty heart is lying still!”.

questions.prompt: Which details make the city seem like countryside?
facilitatorNotes: Ships, towers and temples lie “Open unto the fields, and to the sky”; the air is “smokeless,” because the fires of the day are not yet lit; the sun steeps the city as it would valley, rock or hill. London, usually crowded and smoky, looks like a landscape.
evidence: Open unto the fields, and to the sky;
All bright and glittering in the smokeless air.

questions.prompt: “This City now doth, like a garment, wear / The beauty of the morning.” What does the simile suggest about the beauty?
facilitatorNotes: A garment is put on and taken off, so the beauty may be borrowed from the morning and will not last the day. Another reading: the morning reveals a beauty the city always had but hides under its noise.
evidence: This City now doth, like a garment, wear The beauty of the morning;

questions.prompt: The sonnet ends, “And all that mighty heart is lying still!” Is the city asleep, or is the image more troubling?
facilitatorNotes: The city is a living body whose heart is resting. A still heart can also suggest death, which gives the hush a strange edge. Most readers hear wonder and peace; the double sense adds to the awe.
evidence: Dear God! the very houses seem asleep;
And all that mighty heart is lying still!

readings.title: It is a beauteous evening, calm and free
readings.challenge: Notice how a sonnet turns from a scene to a person.
readings.focus: Reverence felt by an adult, and a child’s holiness that does not need to feel it.
readings.context: William Wordsworth (1770–1850) wrote the poems in this volume between 1798 and 1803; from 1799 he lived with his sister Dorothy at Grasmere in the English Lake District. He wrote this sonnet on the beach at Calais, in France, in August 1802. The girl walking with the speaker is generally identified as Caroline, Wordsworth’s nine-year-old daughter, who lived in France with her mother and whom he met there that summer. “Abraham’s bosom” means heaven, from a parable of Jesus; the Temple’s inner shrine was the holiest part of the Temple in Jerusalem.

excerpt.locator: “It is a beauteous evening, calm and free,” the whole sonnet; opens “It is a beauteous evening, calm and free, The holy time is quiet as a Nun Breathless with…”; closes “…And worshipp'st at the Temple's inner shrine, God being with thee when we know it not.”.

questions.prompt: Find the comparison in the first lines. What does it make the evening feel like?
facilitatorNotes: The evening is “quiet as a Nun / Breathless with adoration”: a stillness full of worship, as if the whole scene were praying.
evidence: The holy time is quiet as a Nun Breathless with adoration;

questions.prompt: “Listen! the mighty Being is awake.” What is the speaker asking the girl to hear?
facilitatorNotes: The sea’s endless sound, “like thunder,” which he hears as the motion of God or of a divine power in nature. In the calm evening something vast is still at work.
evidence: Listen! the mighty Being is awake,
A sound like thunder—everlastingly.

questions.prompt: The girl seems “untouched by solemn thought.” Why does the speaker say her nature is “not therefore less divine”?
facilitatorNotes: He believes a child is close to God without knowing it, while the adult must work at reverence. Some readers find this tender; others think it idealises childhood or excuses a father who barely knows his child. The text supports the tenderness most directly.
evidence: If thou appear untouched by solemn thought, Thy nature is not therefore less divine:
God being with thee when we know it not.

readings.title: To Toussaint L'Ouverture
readings.challenge: Work out what comfort a poet can offer someone whose cause seems lost.
readings.focus: A sonnet that honours a defeated leader of a revolution against slavery.
readings.context: William Wordsworth (1770–1850) wrote the poems in this volume between 1798 and 1803; from 1799 he lived with his sister Dorothy at Grasmere in the English Lake District. Toussaint Louverture (spelled L’Ouverture here), who had been born into slavery, led the revolution in the French colony of Saint-Domingue (now Haiti) that ended slavery there, and became its governor. In 1802 Napoleon’s forces seized him and imprisoned him in France, where he died in April 1803; Haiti declared its independence in 1804. Wordsworth wrote this sonnet in 1802 while Toussaint was a prisoner. A rustic is a farm labourer; the dungeon is “earless” because no one hears a prisoner there.

excerpt.locator: To Toussaint L'Ouverture, the whole sonnet; opens “Toussaint, the most unhappy man of men! Whether the whistling Rustic tend his plough…”; closes “…allies; Thy friends are exultations, agonies, And love, and man's unconquerable mind.”.

questions.prompt: Why does the speaker call Toussaint “the most unhappy man of men”? Where does he imagine him?
facilitatorNotes: He has fallen from leading a people to captivity. Wordsworth does not know whether he is held where he can hear a free labourer whistling at the plough, or in a deep dungeon; either way the contrast with freedom hurts.
evidence: Whether the whistling Rustic tend his plough Within thy hearing,
Pillowed in some deep dungeon's earless den;—

questions.prompt: “Though fallen thyself, never to rise again, / Live, and take comfort.” What comfort can the speaker offer?
facilitatorNotes: That his cause is greater than his body: he has left powers that will keep working for him in air, earth and sky, and in human minds. Readers may find this inspiring, or too easy to say to a man in prison.
evidence: Though fallen thyself, never to rise again, Live, and take comfort.
Powers that will work for thee;

questions.prompt: Who are Toussaint’s “great allies” in the last lines, and why might “agonies” be among them?
facilitatorNotes: Not armies but feelings and powers: triumphs, sufferings, love and “man’s unconquerable mind.” Suffering is an ally because it moves others and keeps the struggle alive. Haiti’s independence in 1804 gives the ending a force Wordsworth could not yet know.
evidence: Thy friends are exultations, agonies, And love, and man's unconquerable mind.

readings.title: London, 1802
readings.challenge: Follow a sonnet that diagnoses a problem in eight lines and offers a model in six.
readings.focus: A call for national renewal through the example of one great writer.
readings.context: William Wordsworth (1770–1850) wrote the poems in this volume between 1798 and 1803; from 1799 he lived with his sister Dorothy at Grasmere in the English Lake District. John Milton (1608–1674), the poet of Paradise Lost, also wrote prose in defence of liberty during England’s civil wars. Wordsworth wrote this in 1802, soon after returning from France. A fen is a marsh; a dower is an inheritance; a bower here is a private room; “manners” means customs and moral habits.

excerpt.locator: London, 1802, the whole sonnet; opens “Milton! thou should'st be living at this hour: England hath need of thee: she is a fen Of…”; closes “…way, In cheerful godliness; and yet thy heart The lowliest duties on herself did lay.”.

questions.prompt: What is wrong with England, according to the speaker? Explain the image of “a fen / Of stagnant waters.”
facilitatorNotes: Nothing moves or flows: church, army, writing, home and wealth have all lost their “inward happiness,” and the English have become selfish. Stagnant water is still, airless and slowly rotting.
evidence: she is a fen Of stagnant waters:
We are selfish men;

questions.prompt: Why Milton? What qualities does the second part of the sonnet give him?
facilitatorNotes: A soul like a star that “dwelt apart,” a voice like the sea, purity and freedom, and yet a heart that took on “the lowliest duties.” He joins greatness with humble service, which is what England lacks.
evidence: Thy soul was like a Star, and dwelt apart:
The lowliest duties on herself did lay.

questions.prompt: The speaker says “We are selfish men,” not “they.” How does that change the tone of the complaint? Can one figure from the past “raise us up”?
facilitatorNotes: He includes himself, so the poem is a confession and a plea rather than a sneer. Readers may doubt that a dead poet can save a nation, but Wordsworth means Milton’s example and writing, which can still be read.
evidence: Oh! raise us up, return to us again;

readings.title: The Solitary Reaper
readings.challenge: Notice how a song the speaker cannot understand becomes more powerful for being unknown.
readings.focus: A passing moment carried away and kept by memory.
readings.context: William Wordsworth (1770–1850) wrote the poems in this volume between 1798 and 1803; from 1799 he lived with his sister Dorothy at Grasmere in the English Lake District. He wrote this after a tour of Scotland with Dorothy in 1803. The Highlands are the mountains of northern Scotland, where many people then spoke Gaelic, which an English traveller could not understand. A reaper cuts grain with a sickle; the Hebrides are islands off Scotland’s west coast; “numbers” are verses; a lay is a song. It is read on Labor Day for its picture of a worker singing at her work.

excerpt.locator: The Solitary Reaper, the whole poem; opens “Behold her, single in the field, Yon solitary Highland Lass! Reaping and singing by…”; closes “…as I mounted up the hill, The music in my heart I bore, Long after it was heard no more.”.

questions.prompt: Why can’t the speaker understand the song? What guesses does he make about it?
facilitatorNotes: She sings in a language he does not know. He guesses at old, unhappy, far-off things and battles, or at some ordinary sorrow that “has been, and may be again.” Not knowing lets the song stand for every kind of sadness.
evidence: Will no one tell me what she sings?
For old, unhappy, far-off things, And battles long ago:

questions.prompt: Look at the two comparisons in the second stanza. Why a nightingale in Arabian sands and a cuckoo in the farthest Hebrides?
facilitatorNotes: Both are welcome sounds in remote places, one hot and one cold, one to tired travellers and one breaking the silence of the sea. Placing the girl’s voice beside these far-off scenes makes it seem rare and enormous.
evidence: Among Arabian sands:
Among the farthest Hebrides.

questions.prompt: The poem begins in the present (“Behold her”) and ends in the past (“I saw her”). What does the change suggest?
facilitatorNotes: The vivid present was a way of reliving the moment; the last stanza admits that it is a memory. The song lasts “Long after it was heard no more,” which is what the poem itself is doing.
evidence: Behold her, single in the field,
The music in my heart I bore, Long after it was heard no more.

readings.title: Hart-Leap Well
readings.challenge: Compare two ways of telling one story: a knight’s triumph and a shepherd’s guesswork years later.
readings.focus: Pride, pleasure and the suffering of an animal; what a ruined place remembers.
readings.context: William Wordsworth (1770–1850) wrote the poems in this volume between 1798 and 1803; from 1799 he lived with his sister Dorothy at Grasmere in the English Lake District. Hart-Leap Well is a spring in Wensleydale, Yorkshire; Wordsworth and Dorothy passed it in December 1799, walking to their new home at Grasmere, and heard the local story. A hart is a male red deer; a vassal is a tenant who owes service to a lord; a courser is a fast horse; a rout is a crowd of riders; to chide is to scold; “yeaned” means born, of a lamb; a rood is about five and a half yards; a paramour is a lover; “sylvan” means of the woods; aspens are trees with trembling leaves; “dolorous” means sorrowful; a furlong is an eighth of a mile; the Swale and the Ure are Yorkshire rivers.
readings.contentNote: A deer is hunted to death and horses and hounds are ridden and run to exhaustion; the death itself is not described.

excerpt.locator: Hart-Leap Well, the whole poem (Part the First and Part the Second); opens “The Knight had ridden down from Wensley Moor With the slow motion of a summer's cloud And…”; closes “…Never to blend our pleasure or our pride With sorrow of the meanest thing that feels."”.

questions.prompt: How does Part the First make the hunt seem glorious? Find one phrase that praises it and one detail that quietly undercuts the praise.
facilitatorNotes: “That glorious day,” the knight flying “like a falcon,” the prancing horse. Against them: a “doleful silence in the air,” the whole company vanished, the dogs stretched out in the fern, and a chase that “looks not like an earthly chase.” The narrator reports the knight’s joy without sharing it.
evidence: Which he had mounted on that glorious day.
There is a doleful silence in the air.

questions.prompt: “I will not stop to tell how far he fled, / Nor will I mention by what death he died.” Why leave this out? What does the poem show instead?
facilitatorNotes: It refuses to make the kill exciting. Instead we see the dead hart with its nostril touching the spring, the water “trembling still” from its last groan, and the three hoof-marks. The stillness speaks, and the knight’s “silent joy” sounds wrong beside it.
evidence: Nor will I mention by what death he died;
The waters of the spring were trembling still.

questions.prompt: What is Sir Walter really celebrating when he builds the pleasure-house, basin and pillars? Compare his promise with what the traveller finds in Part the Second.
facilitatorNotes: His own feat and his own pleasure: he names the place, plans dancing and love there, and turns the hart’s leaps into trophies. He promises the house will last “Till the foundations of the mountains fail”; in Part the Second the trees are dead stumps and the lodge is as hard to find as “a forgotten dream.”
evidence: My mansion with its arbour shall endure;—
Hunt half a day for a forgotten dream.

questions.prompt: How is the Shepherd’s way of telling different from Part the First, and what lesson does the poet draw? Do you accept it?
facilitatorNotes: The Shepherd imagines the hart’s thoughts and life: perhaps born nearby, perhaps drinking here first, coming home to die. He thinks the place is cursed for its sake. The poet agrees that nature mourned the beast and draws a lesson: never mix our pleasure or pride “With sorrow of the meanest thing that feels.” Some readers accept it; others question the curse or note that the poet, too, uses the ruin as a monument to teach.
evidence: And he, perhaps, for aught we know, was born
With sorrow of the meanest thing that feels.

readings.title: The Idle Shepherd-Boys; or, Dungeon-Ghyll Force
readings.challenge: Notice what the characters fail to hear that the reader is told about early.
readings.focus: A dare, a fright and a rescue: play and responsibility on a spring day.
readings.context: William Wordsworth (1770–1850) wrote the poems in this volume between 1798 and 1803; from 1799 he lived with his sister Dorothy at Grasmere in the English Lake District. Dungeon-Ghyll Force is a waterfall in Great Langdale, near Grasmere: a force is a waterfall and a ghyll a ravine. A youngling brood are young birds; “wantonness” here means playful wildness; stag-horn or fox’s tail is club moss; a marge is a bank; a coronal is a wreath; a dam is a mother animal; a rent is a split in rock; “I ween” means I think; to hie is to hurry; to upbraid is to scold. The poet who appears near the end is not named; readers often take him for Wordsworth himself.

excerpt.locator: The Idle Shepherd-Boys; or, Dungeon-Ghyll Force, the whole poem; opens “The valley rings with mirth and joy; Among the hills the echoes play A never never ending…”; closes “…did the Bard Those idle Shepherd-boys upbraid, And bade them better mind their trade.”.

questions.prompt: The first three stanzas are full of sounds. Which sound do the boys fail to hear, and how does the poem prepare us for it?
facilitatorNotes: Echoes, the magpie, the sand-lark, the thrush and the boys’ pipes all sound joyful. At the end of stanza 3 comes the one they “never hear”: a plaintive cry from Dungeon-Ghyll. The reader hears what the boys miss.
evidence: They never hear the cry,
Comes from the depth of Dungeon-Ghyll.

questions.prompt: Why does Walter stop the race, and what dare does he make instead? What does it show about him?
facilitatorNotes: He sees he will lose, so he cries “Stop!” and challenges James to cross the rock bridge over the chasm. Rather than lose, he raises the stakes: competitive, proud and reckless.
evidence: Seeing that he should lose the prize,
Cross, if you dare, where I shall cross—

questions.prompt: On the middle of the arch the challenger hears a moan and nearly collapses. Why is he so frightened, and what is the sound really?
facilitatorNotes: The place is a black, frightful gulf called a “dungeon,” and he is balanced above it; the moan may seem ghostly or a sign of disaster. It is a lamb swept into the pool, answering its mother’s cry. Readers may also say he simply fears falling.
evidence: He totters, pallid as a ghost,
Made answer to that plaintive sound.

questions.prompt: Who rescues the lamb, and how does the poem judge the boys? Is the title fair?
facilitatorNotes: Not the shepherds but a poet “who loves the brooks,” who “gently” tells them to mind their trade. The poem enjoys their play and scolds them mildly, so some readers think “idle” is a light, affectionate label; others note that a lamb nearly drowned while shepherds raced. There is also a joke: a poet, another kind of idler, does the shepherds’ work.
evidence: A Poet, one who loves the brooks
And bade them better mind their trade.

readings.title: The Pet-Lamb
readings.challenge: Separate what the speaker sees and hears from what he imagines.
readings.focus: A child’s care for a tethered lamb, and a poet’s claim to read her heart.
readings.context: William Wordsworth (1770–1850) wrote the poems in this volume between 1798 and 1803; from 1799 he lived with his sister Dorothy at Grasmere in the English Lake District. Barbara Lewthwaite was a real child of Grasmere. The poem’s long lines have six beats. Kine are cattle; “measured numbers” are lines of verse; “bed and board” are a place to sleep and food; covert is shelter; to yean is to give birth to a lamb; a dam is a mother animal; “belike” means perhaps; a fold is a sheep pen.

excerpt.locator: The Pet-Lamb, the whole poem; opens “The dew was falling fast, the stars began to blink; I heard a voice; it said, "Drink,…”; closes “…a look, and she spake with such a tone, That I almost received her heart into my own."”.

questions.prompt: What does the speaker actually see and hear, and what does he imagine? Find the line where he moves from one to the other.
facilitatorNotes: He sees a girl feeding a tethered lamb and hears her say “Drink, pretty creature, drink!”; she walks away, stops, and looks back. Then “Thus, thought I … might sing”: the long song that follows is his imagining of her thoughts, put into verse.
evidence: If Nature to her tongue could measured numbers bring,
Thus, thought I, to her lamb that little Maid might sing:

questions.prompt: In the song, what reasons does the girl give the lamb to be content? Which would matter to a lamb, and which sound like a child’s own hopes?
facilitatorNotes: Soft grass, shade, water and warm milk twice a day, safety from storms and ravens, and rescue by her father. The plan to yoke it to her cart and make it her playmate by the hearth is a child’s dream rather than a lamb’s.
evidence: Then I'll yoke thee to my cart like a pony in the plough;
I bring thee draughts of milk, warm milk it is and new.

questions.prompt: What does she guess at last is troubling the lamb? Why are the mountains both lovely and dangerous in her song?
facilitatorNotes: Perhaps its “mother's heart”: a longing for its wild home and for things she cannot know. The hills look green and fair but hold winds, darkness and brooks that “roar like lions.” She offers safety in place of freedom, and the lamb keeps pulling at its cord.
evidence: That 'tis thy mother's heart which is working so in thee?
When they are angry, roar like lions for their prey.

questions.prompt: At the end the speaker decides how much of the song is hers and how much his. What does he conclude, and why does it matter?
facilitatorNotes: First half and half, then “more than half” hers, because of her look and tone. A poem can be shared between what someone feels and what the poet imagines; the repeated line about receiving “her heart into my own” names that sympathy. Readers may ask whether anyone can really know another person’s thoughts.
evidence: That but half of it was hers, and one half of it was mine.
That I almost received her heart into my own.

readings.title: To Joanna
readings.challenge: Follow a story told inside a letter-like poem, and decide how much of it the speaker claims is true.
readings.focus: A laugh that echoes across the mountains, and a name carved in memory of friendship.
readings.context: William Wordsworth (1770–1850) wrote the poems in this volume between 1798 and 1803; from 1799 he lived with his sister Dorothy at Grasmere in the English Lake District. Joanna Hutchinson was the sister of Mary Hutchinson, whom Wordsworth married in 1802; she had grown up in towns and had been away from Grasmere for two years. This is one of his “Poems on the Naming of Places” (1800). The Rotha is the river through Grasmere; Helm-crag, Hammar-scar, Silver-how, Loughrigg, Fairfield, Helvellyn, Skiddaw, Glaramara and Kirkstone are fells and passes of the Lake District, some many miles apart. Wordsworth later admitted that the echo of Joanna’s laugh is an exaggeration. Runic characters are the letters of ancient Germanic inscriptions; idolatry is worship of idols; to be catechised is to be questioned; broom is a yellow-flowered shrub; ravishment is rapture; the “ancient Woman” on Helm-crag is a rock formation; eighteen moons are eighteen months.

excerpt.locator: To Joanna, the whole poem; opens “Amid the smoke of cities did you pass The time of early youth; and there you learned,…”; closes “…And I, and all who dwell by my fireside, Have called the lovely rock, Joanna's Rock."”.

questions.prompt: Why does the speaker think Joanna may not share his feeling for the hills? How serious is he?
facilitatorNotes: She grew up “Amid the smoke of cities” and learned to love the people by her own fireside, so she is slow to love hills and streams. He calls himself and his household “transgressors in this kind,” a teasing confession that they love nature perhaps too much.
evidence: Amid the smoke of cities did you pass
Yet we, who are transgressors in this kind,

questions.prompt: What does the Vicar accuse him of, and how does he take it?
facilitatorNotes: Of carving a strange name on the rock like a “Runic Priest,” reviving pagan worship. He is “not loth to be so catechised”: the half-teasing, half-loving exchange gives him a reason to tell the story.
evidence: Reviving obsolete idolatry,
I was not loth to be so catechised,

questions.prompt: Why does Joanna laugh, and what happens to her laugh? How does the long list of mountains work?
facilitatorNotes: She laughs at his rapt gazing at the rock. The rock takes up her voice and passes it from fell to fell, Helm-crag to Skiddaw’s “speaking-trumpet” to Kirkstone. The list rolls on like an echo travelling outward, making the whole landscape answer.
evidence: That ravishment of mine, and laughed aloud.
And Kirkstone tossed it from his misty head.

questions.prompt: The speaker is not sure whether the mountains really answered or his ear was “touched / With dreams.” Why leave it open? Why does he carve her name later?
facilitatorNotes: He is sure only “That there was a loud uproar in the hills”: experience and imagination are mixed, and he admits it. Joanna, startled, draws close to him for shelter. Alone eighteen months later, he carves her name “In memory of affections old and true”; readers may see the name as a tribute, or as gentle revenge for her laugh.
evidence: With dreams and visionary impulses
That there was a loud uproar in the hills.
Have called the lovely rock, Joanna's Rock.

readings.title: Point Rash-Judgment (“A narrow girdle of rough stones and crags”)
readings.challenge: Watch a judgment form from distant evidence, then fall apart at close range.
readings.focus: Observation, inference and the duty to judge others charitably.
readings.context: William Wordsworth (1770–1850) wrote the poems in this volume between 1798 and 1803; from 1799 he lived with his sister Dorothy at Grasmere in the English Lake District. This is one of his “Poems on the Naming of Places” (1800), in which he names spots near Grasmere after things that happened there; the “two belovèd Friends” were probably his sister Dorothy and Coleridge. A girdle is a belt; a causeway is a raised path; a copse is a thicket; the “dry wreck” is the line of debris left by the water; the Osmunda is the royal fern; a Naiad is a water nymph of Greek myth, and the Lady of the Mere is the Lady of the Lake from the Arthurian stories; to angle is to fish; “improvident” means careless of the future; a pittance is a tiny amount; admonishment is a warning; a foreland is a headland.

excerpt.locator: “A narrow girdle of rough stones and crags,” from Poems on the Naming of Places, the whole poem; opens “A narrow girdle of rough stones and crags, A rude and natural causeway, interposed…”; closes “…bay Or foreland, on a new-discovered coast; And Point Rash-Judgment is the name it bears.”.

questions.prompt: What are the three friends doing on the shore before they see the man? Which words show their mood?
facilitatorNotes: They saunter, “Played with our time,” watch debris and floating seed-tufts, point out flowers. “Vacant mood” and, later, “happy idleness” show leisure presented as innocent delight.
evidence: Played with our time; and, as we strolled along,
And, in our vacant mood,

questions.prompt: The thistle-down is said to be “Making report of an invisible breeze.” Why might Wordsworth include this small observation before the main event?
facilitatorNotes: Its sudden halts and starts reveal a wind no one can see: a visible sign of a hidden cause. The friends are about to misread a visible figure because they cannot see the hidden cause, his illness. Readers may simply enjoy it as a picture of the calm.
evidence: Making report of an invisible breeze
Suddenly halting now—a lifeless stand!

questions.prompt: What do the friends conclude when they first see the angler, and on what evidence? What do they discover close up?
facilitatorNotes: From a distant figure in a labourer’s clothes fishing during harvest, they judge him lazy and careless, throwing away good wages. Close up he is “worn down / By sickness,” too weak for the harvest, fishing for a pittance. Their facts were right; the fact that mattered was missing.
evidence: The Man must be, who thus can lose a day
Too weak to labour in the harvest field,

questions.prompt: Why do they name the place “Point Rash-Judgment”? What is ironic about who was idle that morning?
facilitatorNotes: To remember the need “to be reserved in speech, / And temper all our thoughts with charity.” The friends themselves were idling while condemning a man for losing a day, and their leisure did not depend on harvest wages. The speaker will not say what they first thought: “I will not say,” which suggests shame.
evidence: The happy idleness of that sweet morn,
And temper all our thoughts with charity.
And Point Rash-Judgment is the name it bears.

readings.title: The Brothers, part 1: the stranger in the churchyard
readings.challenge: Keep track of who knows what, and of who is speaking in a dialogue printed without names.
readings.focus: A homecoming told through a man who will not say who he is.
readings.context: William Wordsworth (1770–1850) wrote the poems in this volume between 1798 and 1803; from 1799 he lived with his sister Dorothy at Grasmere in the English Lake District. The Brothers (1800) is set in Ennerdale, a remote valley in the western Lake District. It opens in the middle of the Priest’s grumbling to his wife Jane. Much of it is dialogue printed without speakers’ names: a new speaker often begins partway through a line, so read for who is talking. The Priest is the vicar of the small parish chapel; to card wool is to comb it between two wire-toothed boards for spinning; shrouds are a ship’s rigging; the Main is the open sea; traffic is trade; the Indian Isles are the East Indies; a pike is a peak; a water-spout is a cloudburst; twenty score is four hundred; “threescore years and ten,” seventy, is the Bible’s span of a life.

excerpt.locator: The Brothers, from the opening to the Priest’s defence of the unmarked graves; opens “These Tourists, heaven preserve us! needs must live A profitable life: some glance along,…”; closes “…The thought of death sits easy on the man Who has been born and dies among the mountains.”.

questions.prompt: The poem opens with the Priest grumbling about tourists. What does he think of them, and what mistake does he make about the stranger?
facilitatorNotes: Tourists flit like butterflies or sit sketching for hours; he takes the man lingering in the churchyard for another “moping Son of Idleness,” a dreamer whom the sunset will brand a fool. In fact the stranger is Leonard, a local shepherd come home from sea. The reader knows more than the Priest from the start.
evidence: But, for that moping Son of Idleness,
Write fool upon his forehead.

questions.prompt: What did Leonard see when he gazed into the sea, and what does it tell us about him?
facilitatorNotes: In the steady trade winds he saw mountains, grazing sheep and shepherds dressed in grey, so vividly it was as if with his “bodily eye.” He was “half a shepherd on the stormy seas”: his heart never left home.
evidence: Was half a shepherd on the stormy seas.
Saw mountains; saw the forms of sheep that grazed

questions.prompt: Why does Leonard go to the churchyard instead of asking about his brother? What does he hope when he finds the new grave?
facilitatorNotes: His heart “Failed in him”: he is afraid of the news, and the graves let him learn without asking. Finding a new grave, he begins to hope he has simply forgotten it, and even imagines the hills themselves have changed. Fear and hope rewrite his memory.
evidence: Failed in him; and, not venturing to enquire
That it was not another grave; but one He had forgotten.

questions.prompt: In the dialogue Leonard hints that he knew the valley long ago, and the Priest defends the unmarked graves. What do you learn from what Leonard says and does not say?
facilitatorNotes: He remembers the old foot-way and the dark cleft and starts to point (“But, surely, yonder—”); the Priest then tells of two springs on the peak, one now gone: an image of two brothers, one lost. He presses the Priest about graves without names, “An orphan could not find his mother's grave,” which is his own fear. The Priest answers that the dead live on in talk by the fireside. Readers may wonder why Leonard still hides who he is.
evidence: There were two springs which bubbled side by side,
An orphan could not find his mother's grave:
We talk about the dead by our fire-sides.

readings.title: The Brothers, part 2: Walter Ewbank and the two orphans
readings.challenge: Listen for the moments when the stranger steers the conversation, and when the Priest misreads him.
readings.focus: Dramatic irony: a man hears his own family’s story told to him as a stranger.
readings.context: Recap: Leonard Ewbank, who left Ennerdale twenty years ago to go to sea, has come home to find his only brother, James. Afraid to ask, he searched the churchyard, where the Priest, not recognising him, has defended the valley’s unmarked graves. Eight-score winters are a hundred and sixty years; “hale fourscore” is a healthy eighty; bonds and mortgages are debts secured on land; burthens are burdens; roe-bucks are small deer; a stripling is a youth; Great Gavel (Great Gable), the Leeza and the Enna are a fell and streams of Ennerdale, and Egremont is a nearby town; the Barbary coast is North Africa, whose pirates enslaved captured sailors.
readings.contentNote: The Priest reports that Leonard was last heard of as a slave on the Barbary coast.

excerpt.locator: The Brothers, the churchyard dialogue from “Your Dalesmen, then” to the account of Leonard at sea; opens “Your Dalesmen, then, do in each other's thoughts Possess a kind of second life: no doubt…”; closes “…he would return, To live in peace upon his father's land, And lay his bones among us.”.

questions.prompt: Who says “'Tis a common case. / We'll take another”? Why does he steer the Priest to the grave beside the rock?
facilitatorNotes: Leonard. He cuts off the story of the broken-hearted man and points to “the last of those three graves,” beside the rock: as it turns out, his grandfather’s. His cool tone hides how urgently he wants to know.
evidence: 'Tis a common case.
Beneath yon ridge, the last of those three graves?

questions.prompt: What kind of man was Walter Ewbank, and why did the family lose their land?
facilitatorNotes: Cheerful and light-footed at eighty; but five generations had struggled with debts on the small farm, each giving up “A little—yet a little,” and Walter sank under “bond, / Interest, and mortgages.” At his death house, land and sheep were sold. Compare Michael’s fear of losing his fields.
evidence: He had the lightest foot in Ennerdale:
Interest, and mortgages; at last he sank,

questions.prompt: What does the Priest remember about Leonard and James as boys? Choose the image that best shows their bond.
facilitatorNotes: Leonard carried his delicate younger brother on his back through flooded fords to school; they were “such darlings of each other”; they bounded over the hills like roe-bucks. Students may choose any of these and explain.
evidence: Bearing his brother on his back. I have seen him,
They were such darlings of each other. Yes,

questions.prompt: The Priest notices the stranger weeping and says the bells will never ring for Leonard. What does the reader understand that the Priest does not?
facilitatorNotes: The stranger is Leonard, weeping at his own story, and the Priest’s “Heaven bless you when you are among your kindred!” hurts because his kindred are in these graves. The Priest believes Leonard enslaved or dead while he stands before him. Readers can discuss why Leonard still keeps silent: fear of the news about James, pride, or shame.
evidence: To hear a stranger talking about strangers,
This is sad talk—they'll never sound for him—

readings.title: The Brothers, part 3: the Pillar
readings.challenge: Notice how indirectly the central question is asked and answered.
readings.focus: Grief, an unspoken name and a homecoming abandoned.
readings.context: Recap: in the churchyard the Priest, not knowing he is speaking to Leonard, has told how the Ewbank brothers, orphans raised by their grandfather, lost their land, and how Leonard went to sea for his brother’s sake and was last heard of as a slave in North Africa. Leonard still has not asked the question he came to ask. A fellow-tale is a matching story; to pine is to waste away with longing; “haply” means perhaps; heath is low moorland shrub; an “unhallowed end” is a death without God’s blessing; disquietude is anxiety; Egremont is a market town near the coast.
readings.contentNote: A young man dies in a fall from a crag (“with mangled limbs”); his brother fears it was suicide, and the Priest believes it was an accident in his sleep.

excerpt.locator: The Brothers, from Leonard’s “If that day / Should come” to the end of the poem; opens “If that day Should come, 'twould needs be a glad day for him; He would himself, no doubt,…”; closes “…who he was. This done, he went on shipboard, and is now A Seaman, a grey-headed Mariner.”.

questions.prompt: Find where Leonard finally asks about his brother. Why does he ask in such a roundabout way?
facilitatorNotes: “You said his kindred all were in their graves, / And that he had one Brother—”: he frames it as a remark about the absent sailor, never as his own question, and does not finish the sentence. He fears the answer and fears being recognised.
evidence: You said his kindred all were in their graves, And that he had one Brother—

questions.prompt: What happened to James after Leonard left? Which detail shows that he never stopped missing his brother?
facilitatorNotes: Delicate, he drooped and pined; the whole dale took him in, “the child of all the dale.” But he began to walk in his sleep, searching for Leonard. Seeing the stranger moved, the Priest apologises for having judged him unkindly.
evidence: He was the child of all the dale—he lived
He sought his brother Leonard.—You are moved!

questions.prompt: Why does Leonard insist “He could not come to an unhallowed end!”? How does the Priest’s account answer him, and how certain is it?
facilitatorNotes: He fears that James, in grief, took his own life. The Priest explains that James probably fell asleep on the Pillar and walked over the edge in his sleep. It is the village’s guess, “we all conjectured,” not certain knowledge. The staff caught on the rock and left to moulder is the poem’s haunting proof of what happened.
evidence: He could not come to an unhallowed end!
That, as the day was warm, he had lain down
It hung;—and mouldered there.

questions.prompt: Leonard says “My Brother!” but the Vicar does not hear. Why does he never tell the Priest who he is, and why does he leave the valley he came home to?
facilitatorNotes: Grief takes away his speech; then the vale where he was happy becomes “A place in which he could not bear to live.” His letter blames “the weakness of his heart.” Readers may see shame, grief, or a feeling that saying his name would make the loss final. The last line shows the sea claiming him for good.
evidence: The Vicar did not hear the words: and now,
He had not dared to tell him who he was.
A Seaman, a grey-headed Mariner.

readings.title: Michael, part 1: the Evening Star
readings.challenge: Follow a slow, patient opening and notice what the narrator asks you to look for.
readings.focus: A shepherd’s love of his land and of his son, built up before anything happens.
readings.context: William Wordsworth (1770–1850) wrote the poems in this volume between 1798 and 1803; from 1799 he lived with his sister Dorothy at Grasmere in the English Lake District. Michael (1800) ends the second volume of Lyrical Ballads; Wordsworth called it a pastoral poem, a poem of shepherd life. Green-head Ghyll is a steep stream above Grasmere: a ghyll is a ravine with a stream. Kites are birds of prey; a dell is a small valley; “appertains” means belongs; a helpmate is a wife; to card wool is to comb it for spinning; flax is the plant linen is made from; pottage is thick soup; to be “overbrowed” is to be overhung; Easedale and Dunmail-Raise are a valley and pass near Grasmere; a coppice is a wood of young trees cut for poles; an urchin is a small child; hire is wages.

excerpt.locator: Michael, from the opening to Luke’s eighteenth year; opens “If from the public way you turn your steps Up the tumultuous brook of Green-head Ghyll,…”; closes “…And now, when he had reached his eighteenth year, He was his comfort and his daily hope.”.

questions.prompt: The narrator begins with directions to a hidden valley. What is there to see, and why does he say you might “notice not”?
facilitatorNotes: Only “a straggling heap of unhewn stones” beside the brook, an object so plain it could be passed by. The story will explain why it matters. He adds that this tale first taught him to feel “For passions that were not my own.”
evidence: Might see and notice not. Beside the brook
Appears a straggling heap of unhewn stones!

questions.prompt: “And grossly that man errs” who thinks the fields and hills meant nothing to Michael. What did they mean to him?
facilitatorNotes: They were like a book that preserved his memories of hardship, skill and courage, of animals he had saved; they had “Strong hold on his affections,” as “The pleasure which there is in life itself.” His land is memory and identity, not just property.
evidence: Which, like a book, preserved the memory
The pleasure which there is in life itself.

questions.prompt: Why was the cottage called “The Evening Star”? What does the name say about the family?
facilitatorNotes: Their lamp burned early and late and could be seen across the vale, “a public symbol” of the couple’s endless work. A star is steady and guiding, and evening suggests the old age of the parents.
evidence: And was a public symbol of the life
Both old and young, was named The Evening Star.

questions.prompt: Why is Luke dearer to Michael than anything else? Find two moments from Luke’s childhood that show their bond.
facilitatorNotes: A child brings an old man “hope … and forward-looking thoughts.” Michael rocked his cradle “as with a woman's gentle hand,” kept him near at the Clipping Tree, made him a shepherd’s staff, and took him to the heights until “the old Man's heart seemed born again.” Notice the narrator’s warning that such hopes bring “stirrings of inquietude.”
evidence: Brings hope with it, and forward-looking thoughts,
His cradle, as with a woman's gentle hand.
And that the old Man's heart seemed born again?

readings.title: Michael, part 2: the forfeiture
readings.challenge: Read a family’s decision through what each person says, and what each keeps silent.
readings.focus: A debt, a plan to save the land, and the hopes and fears in it.
readings.context: Recap: Michael, an old shepherd of Grasmere, his wife Isabel and their only son Luke, now eighteen, live by hard, steady work; their lamp has earned the cottage the name The Evening Star, and Luke is his father’s comfort and hope. To be bound “in surety” is to promise to pay another person’s debt if he cannot; the forfeiture is the sum then owed. Patrimonial fields are land inherited from one’s fathers. A parish-boy was a poor orphan kept by the parish; pedlar’s wares are small goods carried for sale; “forthwith” means at once; jocund means cheerful.

excerpt.locator: Michael, from the “Distressful tidings” to Michael’s consent that Luke shall go; opens “While in this sort the simple household lived From day to day, to Michael's ear there…”; closes “…go, Would surely be forgotten. But at length She gave consent, and Michael was at ease.”.

questions.prompt: What has happened to Michael’s money, and why does he refuse the simplest remedy?
facilitatorNotes: He had guaranteed his nephew’s debts, and now must pay “little less / Than half his substance.” Selling some fields is the obvious answer, but his heart fails: if the land passed to a stranger, he “could not lie quiet in my grave.”
evidence: Than half his substance. This unlooked-for claim,
That I could not lie quiet in my grave.

questions.prompt: How does Michael judge his nephew? Read his words closely: does he forgive him?
facilitatorNotes: He cannot know whether the nephew cheated him: “if he / Were false to us; and if he were not false.” He says “I forgive him,” then breaks off, as if anger and fairness are still fighting; the dashes show the struggle.
evidence: I forgive him;—but 'Twere better to be dumb than to talk thus.

questions.prompt: Isabel sits silent while Michael explains his plan. What is she thinking about, and why does it cheer her?
facilitatorNotes: Richard Bateman, a poor parish-boy sent to London with a basket of goods, who grew rich overseas and built a marble-floored chapel at home: proof a poor boy can make a fortune and still honour his birthplace. It is a hopeful local legend, and nothing promises that Luke is like him.
evidence: There's Richard Bateman, thought she to herself,
And, at his birth-place, built a chapel floored

questions.prompt: Michael goes to the fields “With a light heart,” but Isabel hears him troubled in his sleep. What does the poem show about the gap between a plan and a feeling?
facilitatorNotes: By day he is sure (“If he could go, the Boy should go to-night”); at night his hopes are gone. Isabel begs Luke not to leave, “if thou leave thy Father he will die,” yet Luke’s cheerful answer restores her, and the house seems happy again. Readers can discuss whether the family is hiding its fears, and what Michael’s hurry reveals.
evidence: Heard him, how he was troubled in his sleep:
For if thou leave thy Father he will die.
If he could go, the Boy should go to-night.

readings.title: Michael, part 3: the sheep-fold
readings.challenge: Connect the poem’s ending to its opening, and notice how little the narrator says about the hardest events.
readings.focus: A covenant in stone, a son lost to the city, and what love can endure.
readings.context: Recap: to pay a ruinous debt without selling his inherited land, the old shepherd Michael is sending his only son Luke, now eighteen, to a prosperous kinsman in the city; after some doubts the family has agreed, and Luke leaves tomorrow. A sheep-fold is a walled pen of unmortared stones; “burthened” means mortgaged; a covenant is a solemn agreement; the “family mould” is the family’s burial ground; dissolute means immoral and wild; ignominy is public disgrace.

excerpt.locator: Michael, from the walk to the heap of stones to the end of the poem; opens “Near the tumultuous brook of Green-head Ghyll, In that deep valley, Michael had designed…”; closes “…Of the unfinished Sheep-fold may be seen Beside the boisterous brook of Green-head Ghyll.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Michael ask Luke to lay the first stone of the sheep-fold? What will the unfinished fold mean while Luke is away?
facilitatorNotes: It was “a work for us” and now becomes “a work for me”; Luke’s stone makes it a covenant between them, something to remember when tempted, and a work Luke will find finished on his return: “A work which is not here.”
evidence: Here, lay it for me, Luke, with thine own hands.
A work which is not here: a covenant

questions.prompt: Before the stone, Michael tells Luke “some little part / Of our two histories.” What does he want Luke to remember, and why does Luke sob?
facilitatorNotes: That they were “playmates” from Luke’s infancy, that Michael’s own parents and forefathers lived and died here, and that he toiled forty years to free the land. It sounds like a last testament, and Luke is overcome by how much he is loved.
evidence: But we were playmates, Luke: among these hills,
He sobbed aloud. The old Man grasped his hand,

questions.prompt: How does the narrator tell what happened to Luke? Why use so few lines?
facilitatorNotes: In a few lines: he slackens, falls into “evil courses,” and flees abroad. The city is never shown; the poem’s attention stays with Michael, and the news arrives the way it would in the valley, as a report.
evidence: To slacken in his duty; and, at length,
To seek a hiding-place beyond the seas.

questions.prompt: “And never lifted up a single stone.” Why is this line so often called one of the saddest in English poetry? What does the ending suggest has survived?
facilitatorNotes: The strong old man still works, but at the fold grief stops him; the narrator gives it as what “is believed by all,” the valley’s memory. Love made the loss “endurable.” At the end the land is sold and the cottage ploughed under; only the oak and the stones remain, the same heap of stones the poem began with, so the poem itself becomes the memorial. Readers may find the ending despairing or consoling.
evidence: And never lifted up a single stone.
There is a comfort in the strength of love;
Of the unfinished Sheep-fold may be seen

readings.title: Emma’s Dell (“It was an April morning: fresh and clear”)
readings.challenge: Follow the speaker’s mood from scattered delight to a single chosen place, and listen for the moment the sounds of the valley come together.
readings.focus: How a person makes a place their own without owning it.
readings.context: William Wordsworth (1770–1850) wrote the poems in this volume between 1798 and 1803; from 1799 he lived with his sister Dorothy at Grasmere in the English Lake District. This is the first of his “Poems on the Naming of Places” (1800), in which he gives private names to spots near Grasmere in memory of people he loved; “To Joanna” and “A narrow girdle of rough stones and crags” belong to the same group. “Emma” is generally taken to be his sister Dorothy. A rivulet is a small stream; vernal means of spring; tardy means late; a glen and a dell are narrow valleys; sallies are sudden bursts; a linnet is a small finch; furze is gorse, a yellow-flowered shrub; resplendent means shining.

excerpt.locator: “It was an April morning: fresh and clear,” the first of the Poems on the Naming of Places, the whole poem; opens “It was an April morning: fresh and clear The Rivulet, delighting in its strength, Ran…”; closes “…When they have cause to speak of this wild place, May call it by the name of Emma's Dell.”.

questions.prompt: In the first seventeen lines, what does everything in the valley seem to want? Find two images that make the season impatient, and one that makes it content.
facilitatorNotes: The stream runs “with a young man’s speed”; the budding groves seem eager “to urge on / The steps of June,” as if their colours were only in the way. Yet “an entire contentment” fills the air, and even leafless trees look as if summer were their natural face. Spring here is eager and satisfied at once.
evidence: Ran with a young man's speed
Such an entire contentment in the air

questions.prompt: The speaker roams “in the confusion of my heart, / Alive to all things and forgetting all.” What state of mind is this, and how does the waterfall change it?
facilitatorNotes: An open, unfocused happiness in which he takes everything in and holds on to nothing. At the turn of the glen the waterfall’s “glad sound” gathers the lamb, dog, linnet and thrush into one song, and everything heard before seems mere “common pleasure.” Scattered feeling finds a centre; some readers call this the poem’s turning point.
evidence: I roamed in the confusion of my heart,
Of common pleasure: beast and bird, the lamb,

questions.prompt: The song seems “like the wild growth / Or like some natural produce of the air, / That could not cease to be.” What do these comparisons suggest?
facilitatorNotes: No one composes the music; it grows like a plant out of the place itself. “Could not cease to be” gives a passing moment the feeling of permanence, and that feeling leads to his wish to fix the spot with a name.
evidence: Or like some natural produce of the air,
That could not cease to be.

questions.prompt: Why “Our thoughts at least are ours”? What does naming the dell for Emma give, and why does he imagine shepherds using the name after he is dead?
facilitatorNotes: He owns no land (the only house in view is a distant mountain-cottage), but his thoughts and his gift of a name are his own. The name costs nothing, makes the place “my other home,” and may outlive them both, though “perhaps” keeps the hope modest. The poem itself is what makes the name last. Some readers find the gesture tender; others find it a little possessive of a place shepherds already know.
evidence: Our thoughts at least are ours; and this wild nook,
May call it by the name of Emma's Dell.

readings.title: The Farmer of Tilsbury Vale
readings.challenge: Decide what the speaker wants you to think of Adam, and notice how he heads off a harsher judgment.
readings.focus: A countryman who has done wrong, and the country that stays in his heart in the city.
readings.context: William Wordsworth (1770–1850) wrote the poems in this volume between 1798 and 1803; from 1799 he lived with his sister Dorothy at Grasmere in the English Lake District. Old Adam is a ruined farmer who has fled his debts to London. Corn-land is grain-land and lea is grassland; a wight is a fellow; pelf is money; “I ween” means I think; to demur is to hesitate; to hie is to hurry. Covent Garden was London’s great fruit and flower market, the Haymarket a street where hay was sold from waggons, Smithfield the cattle market, and the Strand a busy street.

excerpt.locator: The Farmer of Tilsbury Vale, the whole poem; opens “'Tis not for the unfeeling, the falsely refined, The squeamish in taste, and the narrow…”; closes “…that thy grave, wheresoever it be, Will hear the wind sigh through the leaves of a tree.”.

questions.prompt: The first stanza says who the poem is not for. Why would Wordsworth begin by warning off “the narrow of mind”?
facilitatorNotes: Because Adam has done something a narrow judge would condemn, and the speaker wants readers ready to look past it. The warning makes sympathy a test of the reader.
evidence: 'Tis not for the unfeeling, the falsely refined,
That I sing of old Adam, the pride of old men.

questions.prompt: What exactly did Adam do wrong? How does the speaker describe it, and how does he excuse it?
facilitatorNotes: He borrowed from all his neighbours, paid back what he could, kept something back, and left without a word. The speaker admits the “sin and the shame” but says Adam did it “all in the ease of his heart,” without scheming. Readers may find the excuse generous or too easy: the neighbours still lost their money.
evidence: Turned his back on the country—and off like a bird.
In him it was scarcely a business of art,

questions.prompt: How has London changed Adam? Find the details that make him seem young again.
facilitatorNotes: Poverty forces him into every trade, yet he seems “ten birthdays younger”; his fingers are busy as bees; the city surprises him like a stranger, and he trembles “like a maiden of twenty.” Need makes him alert, and his feeling for nature makes everything new.
evidence: He seems ten birthdays younger, is green and is stout;
Full ten times a day takes his heart by surprise.

questions.prompt: In the last stanzas Adam visits the hay-waggons and Smithfield. What does he find there, and what does the closing wish for his grave add?
facilitatorNotes: He smells the hay, thinks of the fields he mowed, breathes the cows’ breath, and his heart is “in Tilsbury Vale.” The city keeps scraps of the country that feed his memory. The final wish gives him in death a blade of grass and a tree, the country he left. Some readers find it tender; others notice that the poem never returns him home.
evidence: And his heart all the while is in Tilsbury Vale.
May one blade of grass spring over thy head;

readings.title: Alice Fell; or, Poverty
readings.challenge: Follow a night journey told by a traveller, and notice how much grief a small object can carry.
readings.focus: A child’s loss that looks small to everyone but her.
readings.context: William Wordsworth (1770–1850) wrote the poems in this volume between 1798 and 1803; from 1799 he lived with his sister Dorothy at Grasmere in the English Lake District. A post-boy drives hired horses; a chaise is a light travelling carriage; the nave is the hub of a wheel; Durham is a city in the north of England; duffil (duffel) is a thick woollen cloth.

excerpt.locator: Alice Fell; or, Poverty, the whole poem; opens “The post-boy drove with fierce career, For threatening clouds the moon had drowned; When,…”; closes “…as man can sell!" Proud creature was she the next day, The little orphan, Alice Fell!”.

questions.prompt: How does the speaker discover Alice? Why does Wordsworth make him hear the sound several times before he finds her?
facilitatorNotes: The cry seems to follow the chaise, stops when they stop, returns when they drive on. The repetition builds a mystery and shows that the speaker keeps listening when the post-boy would drive on.
evidence: It seemed to follow with the chaise,
The cry, I bade him halt again.

questions.prompt: What is the cloak like, and why does Alice weep so bitterly over it?
facilitatorNotes: It is “a miserable rag,” like a scarecrow’s. For an orphan it may be nearly all she owns, and losing it is losing her only protection; the speaker says her grief seemed endless, as if she had lost “her only friend.”
evidence: A weather-beaten rag as e'er
As if she had lost her only friend

questions.prompt: Alice says only a few things. What does she choose to tell the speaker, and what does that suggest about her?
facilitatorNotes: “My cloak!”, “Look here!”, “To Durham”, then her name and that she is “fatherless and motherless,” and that she belongs to Durham. She checks herself in her distress to answer properly: a child used to looking after herself.
evidence: I'm fatherless and motherless.
She checked herself in her distress,

questions.prompt: The poem’s other title is “Poverty,” but it ends with a proud girl in a new cloak. Is this a happy ending?
facilitatorNotes: One gift solves one night’s grief: Alice is “Proud creature” the next day. But she is still an orphan walking lonely roads, and the speaker leaves her at the inn. Some readers find the ending warm; others find it shows how little charity can change.
evidence: To buy a new cloak for the old.
Proud creature was she the next day,

readings.title: Beggars, and its Sequel
readings.challenge: Compare a poem of first impressions with the poem the poet wrote later about the same people.
readings.focus: Begging, lying and beauty, and a later wish that children met by chance came to no harm.
readings.context: William Wordsworth (1770–1850) wrote the poems in this volume between 1798 and 1803; from 1799 he lived with his sister Dorothy at Grasmere in the English Lake District. “Egyptian” was the old word for the Romani people (once called Gypsies), wrongly thought to come from Egypt; the Amazons were warrior women of Greek legend; an alms or a boon is a gift to a beggar; a weed here is a wild plant; a suppliant is someone begging; Aurora is the goddess of the dawn, whose chariot (car) flowers go before; “dædal” means skilfully made; a bane is a curse.
readings.contentNote: The speaker describes a Romani woman as exotic and “a weed of glorious feature,” and assumes the begging is a trick; these are an English traveller’s period views.

excerpt.locator: Beggars and Sequel to the Foregoing, both poems whole; opens “She had a tall man's height or more; Her face from summer's noontide heat No bonnet…”; closes “…of deadly injury? Destined, whate'er their earthly doom, For mercy and immortal bloom?”.

questions.prompt: How does the speaker describe the woman? Which details make her seem more like a queen than a beggar?
facilitatorNotes: She is very tall, haughty, in a long flowing mantle and a snow-white cap, fit to lead Amazons; he gives her money because she “was beautiful to see.” He also doubts her story at once, calling such woes impossible in England.
evidence: fit person for a Queen
Such woes, I knew, could never be;

questions.prompt: What happens when the boys say their mother is dead? Who do you believe, and why?
facilitatorNotes: The speaker scolds them for lying; they show no shame and run off to play. The boys’ face matches the woman’s, so he is probably right, but the poem never proves it; some readers think the speaker’s certainty is itself worth questioning.
evidence: That cannot be," one answered—"she is dead:"
I looked reproof—they saw—but neither hung his head.

questions.prompt: In “Beggars,” how do the boys at play look to the speaker before they beg? What two pictures of them does the poem hold together?
facilitatorNotes: Chasing a butterfly with flowers in their hats, they seem fit for the finest tasks, like spirits of the dawn; a moment later they beg with “a plaintive whine.” The poem keeps both: free, joyful children and practised beggars.
evidence: Chasing a crimson butterfly;
Each ready with a plaintive whine!

questions.prompt: The Sequel asks “Where are they now?” What does the speaker hope for the boys, and why does he admit his faith may “deceive”?
facilitatorNotes: He cannot know (“all is dark between!”); he hopes the spirits of beauty and the care of heaven kept them from “deadly injury.” He admits that his happy faith on a spring day may not match their real lives, so he turns it into a prayer. Readers may find the hope moving, or think it avoids asking what poverty did to them.
evidence: I ask—but all is dark between!
Or, if such faith must needs deceive—

readings.title: Four Sonnets of September 1802
readings.challenge: Read four sonnets as a sequence, and trace how the speaker’s feeling about his country changes from the first to the last.
readings.focus: Coming home: joy, pity, fear and disappointment in one month.
readings.context: William Wordsworth (1770–1850) wrote the poems in this volume between 1798 and 1803; from 1799 he lived with his sister Dorothy at Grasmere in the English Lake District. In August 1802, during a short peace between Britain and France, Wordsworth and his sister spent a month at Calais; these sonnets were written as they came home. France had just ordered people of African descent out of the country. A sonnet has fourteen lines; Kent is the county around Dover; to “mock the Outcast” is to make her state seem cruelly ironic; rapine is plunder; “the good old cause” was a name for the cause of the English republicans of the 1640s and 1650s; “drest for show” means made only for display.
readings.contentNote: The second sonnet calls a Black woman expelled from France “a white-robed Negro” and speaks of her “tropic fire,” period words and images; the poem’s sympathy is for “this afflicted Race.”

excerpt.locator: Composed in the Valley near Dover, on the Day of Landing; September 1, 1802; September, 1802, near Dover; Written in London, September, 1802; the four sonnets whole; opens “Here, on our native soil, we breathe once more. The cock that crows, the smoke that…”; closes “…Is gone; our peace, our fearful innocence, And pure religion breathing household laws.”.

questions.prompt: In the first sonnet, what sights and sounds make the speaker feel he is home? Why are they such ordinary things?
facilitatorNotes: A cock crowing, curling smoke, bells, boys in white-sleeved shirts playing, waves on chalk: “All, all are English.” Home is felt in ordinary sounds and sights rather than great buildings; their plainness is why they move him.
evidence: The cock that crows, the smoke that curls, that sound
All, all are English.

questions.prompt: What does the speaker notice about the woman in “September 1, 1802,” and what does he ask at the end?
facilitatorNotes: She is finely dressed but downcast, silent, “destitute … of hope or aim,” yet her eyes keep their fire; her rich clothes only “mock the Outcast.” He calls on Heaven and Earth to feel for her people. Students may notice that he observes her closely but never speaks with her, and may discuss his period words.
evidence: Yet downcast as a woman fearing blame;
And feel, thou Earth, for this afflicted Race!

questions.prompt: In “near Dover,” why does the narrow Channel frighten the speaker? What does he finally say protects a nation?
facilitatorNotes: France looks “frightful” near, and the strip of water seems weak; yet winds and waters are “nothing” in themselves. Only virtue and wisdom keep nations great and free. The sonnet turns from physical defence to moral defence.
evidence: The coast of France—the coast of France how near!
Only, the Nations shall be great and free.

questions.prompt: How does the last sonnet’s judgment of England differ from the joy of the first? Which line states the change most sharply?
